related_questions.question: How do you treat multiple sclerosis seizures?

text_blocks.snippet: Seizures in people with multiple sclerosis (MS) are often mild and can be effectively managed with antiepileptic medications (ASMs). These medications help to control or eliminate seizures, and some can also help with other MS symptoms like pain and tremors.

list.title: Antiepileptic Medications (ASMs):
list.snippet: A variety of ASMs are available, with some commonly used examples including carbamazepine (Tegretol), gabapentin (Neurontin), valproic acid (Depakote), and topiramate (Topamax).

list.title: Ketogenic Diet:
list.snippet: While medications are the primary treatment, a ketogenic diet may be helpful for some individuals with MS and seizures.

list.title: Other Treatments:
list.snippet: If medications are not effective, other treatments like surgery or alternative medications may be considered.

list.title: MS and Seizures:
list.snippet: Seizures in MS can be linked to the disease itself, potentially due to demyelination or inflammation.

list.title: Monitoring:
list.snippet: It's important for doctors to carefully monitor patients with MS when prescribing ASMs, as some can cause side effects that mimic MS symptoms.

list.title: Individualized Treatment:
list.snippet: The best treatment approach will depend on the individual's specific circumstances, including their age, sex, other health conditions, and medications they are taking, according to MyMSTeam.

list.title: Lifestyle:
list.snippet: Getting enough sleep, managing stress, and maintaining a healthy lifestyle can also play a role in managing seizures.

text_blocks.snippet: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is a genetic disorder that can cause seizures. Treatment options include anti-seizure medications, ketogenic diet, and in some cases, surgery. Everolimus and vigabatrin are also used to manage seizures associated with TSC.
snippet_highlighted_words: anti-seizure medications, ketogenic diet, and in some cases, surgery

list.title: Anti-seizure medications (ASMs):
list.snippet: A variety of ASMs are used to manage seizures in TSC. Vigabatrin is often used for infantile spasms associated with TSC, but it can have side effects like vision loss, according to UCSF Benioff Children's Hospitals. Other ASMs, such as valproate, lamotrigine, and levetiracetam, may be effective for different types of seizures in TSC.

list.title: Everolimus:
list.snippet: This medication is approved for TSC-associated seizures and can help reduce the frequency and severity of seizures.

list.title: Ketogenic diet:
list.snippet: A high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet can help reduce seizures in some individuals with TSC.

list.title: Surgery:
list.snippet: If a specific seizure focus can be identified through brain imaging and EEG, surgery to remove that area may be an option to eliminate or significantly reduce seizures.

list.title: Responsive Neurostimulation (RNS):
list.snippet: This involves implanting a device that can detect and respond to abnormal brain activity associated with seizures, potentially shortening or stopping them.

list.title: Cannabidiol (CBD):
list.snippet: CBD is used to treat seizures associated with various conditions, including TSC.

list.title: Early intervention:
list.snippet: Starting treatment early, even before seizures manifest, can be crucial in managing TSC and its associated seizures.

list.title: Multidisciplinary care:
list.snippet: Managing TSC requires a team of specialists, including neurologists, geneticists, and other healthcare professionals, to address the various aspects of the condition.

list.title: Ongoing management:
list.snippet: TSC and its associated seizures often require long-term management, even if seizures are well-controlled with treatment.
